definition: Figurehead means a leader in title only, without real power.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word figurehead. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know figurehead should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Everyone photographs the parade marshal waving from the lead car, but the marshal is a figurehead; the parade office plans every float and street closure.
A deputy already outranks a figurehead where it counts: the deputy's power is borrowed, but it is real, while the figurehead's grand title commands nothing.
The autocrat stands at the ladder's far end from the figurehead: every decision in the realm flows from the autocrat personally, while the figurehead decides nothing at all.

A puppet is a leader actively operated by someone hidden behind him: the strings are pulled, the lines are fed, the decisions arrive pre-made. A figurehead is emptier but freer — the title carries no power, yet no one is working him. A figurehead is left alone with an empty title; a puppet never is.

A mouthpiece exists to deliver someone else's words aloud — a spokesperson reading the official line — and claims no leadership of his own. A figurehead holds a genuine title of leadership that simply commands nothing. A mouthpiece is defined by whose words he speaks; a figurehead, by the power his title lacks.
the person a whole operation actually turns on
a leader whose orders are obeyed in fact, not just printed on the letterhead

Figurehead means a leader in title only, without real power.

The awards academy elects a celebrated actor as its president every two years, and every two years the actor learns the same lesson: the president is a figurehead who hands out envelopes, while the academy's paid staff choose the rules, the dates, and the budget.

Figurehead is exact where 'weak leader' is vague: a figurehead may be beloved, dignified, even useful at ceremonies — what defines the role is that the title carries no real power, because the power sits somewhere else.
Call a leader a figurehead when the title is real but the power is not: ceremonial monarchs, honorary presidents, chairmen kept for the letterhead.

If someone behind the scenes actively works the leader like a marionette, puppet is the harsher, more accusing word; and the true holder of power — the potentate of this unit — is what the figurehead only appears to be.

Every spring, Port Alders elects a Harbormaster with sashes, speeches, and a brass bell handed down since 1902.
The winner rings the bell at the regatta, greets the ferries in uniform, and appears on the town's postcards.
What the Harbormaster does not do is run the harbor: berths, fees, and dredging are settled by a port authority in the county seat that has never once consulted him.
When a reporter asked the current holder whether the post was a figurehead, he laughed and rang the bell twice.
'The title is older than the authority, so they let us keep the uniform.
I command the postcards and nothing else.'
